strings.name: Olaf Scholz
strings.role: Former German chancellor and member of the Bundestag
strings.summary: Olaf Scholz is a German Social Democratic politician who served as Hamburg's First Mayor, federal finance minister and vice-chancellor, and federal chancellor. In 2021 he formed a coalition of the SPD, Greens and FDP, facing Russia's war against Ukraine, energy pressures and budget disputes. After the coalition collapsed, he lost a confidence vote; he handed over the chancellorship in 2025 and remained a member of the Bundestag.
strings.coverageNote: Information checked through 18 November 2026. Caretaker service beginning on 25 March 2025 is distinguished from the 6 May handover. Recent activity is supported by a 17 November report of his Hamburg speech the previous evening. Political commitments, his own assessments and implemented policies are distinguished.
strings.influence.rationale: As German chancellor and finance minister, he participated in European financial governance, responses to the energy crisis and changes in policy toward Ukraine.
strings.facts.f1.label: Birth and legal training
strings.facts.f1.value: Born in Osnabrück on 14 June 1958. He studied law in Hamburg from 1978 to 1984, performed alternative civilian service in 1984–1985 and worked as a lawyer from 1985. His legal career does not establish a doctoral qualification.
strings.facts.f2.label: Party and parliamentary career
strings.facts.f2.value: He joined the SPD in 1975 and served in the Bundestag in 1998–2001, 2002–2011 and from 2021. His current parliamentary page lists him as the directly elected member for Brandenburg constituency 061; he is no longer the incumbent chancellor.
strings.highlights.h1.title: Raising the statutory minimum wage
strings.highlights.h1.text: The Bundestag passed his coalition government's bill in June 2022, increasing the statutory minimum wage to €12 an hour from 1 October. This raised an existing wage floor: Germany's nationwide statutory minimum wage had begun in 2015. The €12 figure is not presented as the rate in force in 2026.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Discussing Ukraine policy after leaving office
strings.highlights.h2.text: German public broadcasting reported that he spoke at Haus Rissen in Hamburg on the evening of 16 November 2026, advocating continued support for Ukraine and defending his government's military aid policy. The report appeared on 17 November; assessments of the war and policy effects are attributed to him.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Handing over the chancellorship to Merz
strings.timeline.t1.text: After the new Bundestag convened on 25 March, he received his dismissal certificate and continued government business at the president's request. He handed over to Friedrich Merz on 6 May, ending caretaker service. Leaving the chancellorship did not mean leaving the Bundestag.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Losing the Bundestag confidence vote
strings.timeline.t2.text: Following the coalition's collapse in November, he sought a vote of confidence. With 207 votes in favour, 394 against and 116 abstentions, he fell short of the required majority. This was the confidence procedure under Article 68 of the Basic Law, not impeachment or immediate removal that day.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Constitutional court rejects budget reallocation
strings.timeline.t3.text: The Federal Constitutional Court declared the Second Supplementary Budget Act 2021 void. It concerned transferring €60 billion in unused pandemic borrowing authorisations to the Energy and Climate Fund. This was constitutional review of budget legislation, not a criminal judgment against Scholz personally.
strings.timeline.t4.title: Delivering the Zeitenwende speech
strings.timeline.t4.text: After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, he outlined a shift in security policy in the Bundestag and proposed a one-off €100 billion special fund for the Bundeswehr. Financing and equipment plans in the speech do not mean all funds were spent or equipment delivered that day.
strings.timeline.t5.title: Elected federal chancellor
strings.timeline.t5.text: The Bundestag elected him chancellor with 395 votes, followed by appointment by the federal president. He led a coalition of the SPD, Greens and FDP. This was parliamentary election of a chancellor, not a direct popular election of the head of state.
strings.timeline.t6.title: Becoming finance minister and vice-chancellor
strings.timeline.t6.text: He joined Angela Merkel's fourth cabinet as federal finance minister and vice-chancellor, serving until 2021. His brief period as acting SPD chair in 2018 was a separate party role.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Becoming Hamburg's First Mayor
strings.timeline.t7.text: After the SPD won a majority of seats in Hamburg's early parliamentary election, he was elected First Mayor and served until 2018. This office heads the city-state government and is distinct from the federal chancellorship.
strings.timeline.t8.title: Joining the federal labour ministry
strings.timeline.t8.text: He served as federal minister of labour and social affairs from 2007 to 2009. Previously he had been SPD general secretary and parliamentary manager of its Bundestag group. This phase preceded his terms as Hamburg mayor and finance minister.
